title: The truths, closed
hookLine: four truths, three turns, twelve links
last: DHAMMA — THE SEEING IS THE REAL THING.

cards: At the end of a long hike, some people turn around at the trailhead and look back up at the mountain. From down here it looks small, a single shape against the sky.
But the hiker remembers every switchback: where the path got steep, where they sat on a rock, where the view opened.

Three weeks ago, year two began at an elephant's footprint, with Sariputta saying that every wholesome thing fits inside four truths. Today, a look back up at those four, before the path turns toward the eight.

teach.b: Here's the whole block. The elephant's footprint, the print that holds all others, and a physician's pattern: illness, cause, cure, treatment.
The first truth in full: birth, aging, sickness, death, not getting what you want. Three kinds of dukkha: pain, change, and the unease of made things. Its task: to be understood.
The second truth, samudaya, three thirsts, and its task: to be let go, like a wish that ends at the park. The third, nirodha: it can stop, the burden set down. Nibbana, the fire gone out.
Its task: to be realized, tasted like the ocean's salt. The fourth, magga, the eightfold path, and its task: to be developed, walked into being.
Three turns and twelve aspects: the Buddha's own checklist before he claimed awakening. A handful of leaves: only what helps. Salla: treat the wound first.

Kacchapa: a rare life, so look into the truths. And underneath it all, paticcasamuppada, this because of that, laid out in twelve links, with a seam between feeling and craving where the chain can break.
Seeing that is seeing the Dhamma.

The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, gathers the four truths into a single line: "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain."
One way to read the list: three of the four truths are set up for the last one.

teach.h: THIS BECAUSE OF THAT, IN TWELVE LINKS.
teach.b: Understand, let go, realize: all of it gets done by walking.
Block B takes the eightfold path one factor at a time, starting tomorrow with how the eight fit together.

how: Buddhist schools teach the four noble truths as a core of the Dhamma; in Theravada communities the first sermon, which sets them out, is often chanted in Pali, notably on the full moon of Asalha.

games.q: match each piece of the block to what it taught.

s: each of the four truths has the same task
understand, let go, realize, develop: one verb each.
the Dhammapada sums up the four truths in one line
in Müller's version: pain, its origin, its destruction, and the eightfold holy way.
dependent arising has nothing to do with the four truths
it shows how dukkha arises from conditions and how it can end.

games.q: you've walked all four truths. understand, let go, realize, develop. which one of these is done by walking?
o: the fourth, and through it, the other three.
games.why: the path is the one truth to be developed, and walking it is how dukkha gets understood, craving let go, and the ending realized.

practice: On the first breath, think: dukkha, to be understood. On the second, craving, to be let go; on the third, its ending, to be realized; on the fourth, the path, to be developed.
Then let the words fall away and sit inside the shape they make, like resting at the trailhead.

wordCard.voice: The truths. The four noble truths, each with its task, known in three turns, and resting on dependent arising: the elephant's footprint, walked all the way around.

orig.note: Pali ariyasacca: noble truth; the four ariyasaccāni are the heart of the first sermon.

carryVoice: Your line: four truths, one path. The fourth is the one you can walk today. See you on the path tomorrow.
